title: Low-Carbon Bank Financing Tops $1 Trillion, Nears Fossil Fuels | BloombergNEF
gist: Global banks arranged $0.97 of low-carbon energy financing for every dollar of fossil-fuel financing in 2025 (up from 0.95:1), with total energy supply financing up 15% to $2.3 trillion, but the ratio still sits far below the ~4:1 pace BNEF says is needed this decade -- and the aggregate improvement masks a sharp regional and bank-level split: China and Europe tilting low-carbon (especially on a capex basis), North America tilting harder into fossil fuels.

themes.theme: The Headline Ratio and What It Hides

insights.claim: Global banks arranged $0.97 of low-carbon energy supply financing for every dollar of fossil-fuel financing in 2025, an Energy Supply Banking Ratio (ESBR) of 0.97:1, up only marginally from 0.95:1 in 2024.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Near-parity is a milestone headline, but the pace of improvement (roughly 2 percentage points a year) is glacial relative to what's needed -- don't read parity as a turning point in bank capital allocation.
insights.quote: Global banks arranged $0.97 of low-carbon energy supply finance for every dollar of fossil-fuel financing in 2025
insights.locator: opening paragraph

insights.claim: BloombergNEF states the ESBR needs to average roughly 4:1 (low-carbon to fossil-fuel financing) this decade for bank financing flows to align with climate goals, meaning the current 0.97:1 ratio is far below the required trajectory.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: This is BNEF's benchmark for judging bank climate alignment -- useful as a standing yardstick to track whether real capital reallocation is happening or just marginal drift.
insights.quote: remains far below the average 4:1 Energy Supply Banking Ratio (ESBR) needed this decade to align with climate goals
insights.locator: opening paragraph

insights.claim: Total global energy supply financing tracked by BNEF (recourse debt, public equity, project finance and tax equity) reached $2.3 trillion in 2025, up 15% from 2024, with fossil-fuel volumes at $1.19 trillion and low-carbon volumes at a five-year high of $1.15 trillion.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Both sides of the energy transition are growing in absolute dollar terms simultaneously -- financing isn't a zero-sum shift away from fossil fuels yet, it's an expansion of total energy capex with low-carbon growing modestly faster.
insights.quote: Elevated oil and gas financing... pushed fossil-fuel volumes up to $1.19 trillion. Low-carbon financing grew faster, however, reaching a five-year high of $1.15 trillion, boosted by grid financing.
insights.locator: second paragraph on aggregate volumes

insights.claim: Low-carbon energy financing grew 16% between 2024 and 2025, outpacing overall energy financing growth of 15% and fossil-fuel growth, driven primarily by grid financing rather than generation assets like solar or wind alone.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Grid infrastructure (transmission, distribution, storage buildout) is quietly the dominant growth driver in low-carbon finance -- investors should track grid operators and equipment suppliers, not just generation developers.
insights.locator: key takeaways box

insights.claim: Despite the shift toward low-carbon financing on aggregate, fossil-fuel investment still rose in absolute terms in 2025, showing that the energy transition in bank financing is additive rather than substitutive so far.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Investors betting on fossil-fuel financing decline as a near-term catalyst should recalibrate -- aggregate fossil financing is still climbing, just growing slower than low-carbon.
insights.quote: Despite a shift toward low-carbon energy, fossil-fuel investment still rose in aggregate terms.
insights.locator: second paragraph on aggregate volumes

insights.claim: JPMorgan Chase was the largest bank globally by energy-supply financing volume in 2025 with about $100 billion, but its ESBR fell to 0.63:1 due to rising US fossil-fuel financing combined with a slight drop in low-carbon financing.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: The single largest energy financier in the world is moving its book more fossil-heavy, not less -- a data point for ESG-screened funds and proxy voting campaigns targeting JPMorgan's energy financing disclosures.
insights.quote: JPMorgan Chase was the largest bank by financing volume with about $100 billion in 2025. Its ratio fell to 0.63:1
insights.locator: section 1, largest banks shifted back to fossil fuels

insights.claim: MUFG ranked second-largest globally in energy-supply financing with $77 billion in 2025, and its ESBR also declined due to greater fossil-fuel activity, particularly in the US.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Two of the top two global energy financiers both moved toward fossil fuels in the same year -- suggests a broader pull-back among the largest US-exposed banks rather than an idiosyncratic JPMorgan issue.
insights.locator: section 1, largest banks shifted back to fossil fuels

insights.claim: Bank of China had the highest ESBR among the world's biggest energy-financing banks in 2025 at 1.84:1, up sharply from 1.04:1 in 2024 and 0.58:1 in 2021, making it the only top-10 bank with sustained year-on-year ratio improvement.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Bank of China stands out as the one major global bank with a multi-year, structural trend toward low-carbon financing -- a differentiated name for investors screening for genuine (not one-off) transition alignment among large banks.
insights.quote: Bank of China was the institution with the highest ESBR in 2025 among the list of biggest banks, with a ratio of 1.84:1 – rocketing up from 1.04:1 in 2024.
insights.locator: section 1, largest banks shifted back to fossil fuels

insights.claim: Bank of China's rising ratio is driven mainly by grid financing, and the article expects this momentum to continue because State Grid Corporation of China already issued an additional $61 billion in debt through the first half of 2026, with Bank of China as a main facilitator of that debt.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Forward-looking signal: Bank of China's transition-aligned ratio is likely to stay elevated through 2026 on the back of already-issued State Grid debt -- a near-term catalyst that's already locked in rather than speculative.
insights.quote: Bank of China's involvement should keep its ratio elevated.
insights.locator: section 1, largest banks shifted back to fossil fuels

themes.theme: Regional Split: China and Europe Diverge From North America

insights.claim: China's regional ESBR jumped to 1.6:1 in 2025 as grid financing surged and oil and gas financing volumes declined, with State Grid Corporation of China alone issuing over $105 billion in grid financing in 2025, up $67 billion from 2024.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: China's transition-finance tilt is concentrated in a single dominant issuer (State Grid) -- investors tracking China's energy transition should watch State Grid's debt issuance calendar as a leading indicator for the region's ratio.
insights.quote: China's ESBR jumped to 1.6:1 in 2025, as grid financing surged; State Grid Corporation of China issued over $105 billion in grid financing in 2025, up $67 billion from 2024.
insights.locator: section 2, China and Europe tilt low-carbon

insights.claim: Europe retained the highest ESBR of any region in 2025, rising to 2.5:1 from 2.3:1 in 2024, driven by 75% year-on-year growth in wind-project financing that came largely from offshore wind project finance.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Offshore wind project finance is the single fastest-growing pocket of European bank energy lending -- relevant for European offshore wind developers, turbine makers, and project-finance banks positioning for continued growth.
insights.quote: A 75% year-on-year growth in financing for wind projects boosted its ratio, largely from offshore wind project finance.
insights.locator: section 2, China and Europe tilt low-carbon

insights.claim: North America moved in the opposite direction from China and Europe: it remained the world's largest financing market at $973 billion in 2025, but fossil-fuel financing rose by $92 billion versus only $8 billion for low-carbon, pushing the region's ESBR down to 0.5:1.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: North America -- the single biggest energy-financing market globally -- is the clearest laggard region and the main drag on the global ratio; a contrarian signal against assuming global bank capital is broadly rotating to clean energy.
insights.quote: Fossil-fuel financing increased by $92 billion, compared with only $8 billion for low-carbon financing. This pushed the region's ratio down to 0.5:1 in 2025
insights.locator: section 2, North America backs fossil fuels

insights.claim: US bank financing for companies with coal-related revenue exposure rose to record levels in 2025, reaching $42 billion, underscoring the US as the main driver of North America's declining ESBR.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: A record level of US coal-exposure financing runs counter to the broader narrative of declining coal investment -- worth flagging for investors tracking bank coal-financing policies and potential reputational/regulatory risk.
insights.quote: Financing in the US for companies with coal-related revenue exposure increased to record levels, at $42 billion.
insights.locator: section 2, North America backs fossil fuels

themes.theme: Capex vs. Revenue: A Different Lens on Bank Alignment

insights.claim: When BNEF adjusts the ESBR based on company capital expenditure rather than revenue exposure, the ratio rises to 1.32:1 in 2025, notably higher than the 0.97:1 revenue-based ratio, implying banks have facilitated more low-carbon than fossil-fuel financing on a capex basis in every year since 2022.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: The revenue-based ratio (the headline, backward-looking metric) understates the transition already underway in borrower business models -- the capex lens is arguably the more forward-looking signal for where bank-financed capital is actually going next.
insights.quote: The capex-based ratio sits at 1.32:1 in 2025, higher than the 0.97:1 revenue-based result... banks have facilitated more low-carbon than fossil-fuel financing every year since 2022.
insights.locator: section 3, capex reveals low-carbon financing tilt

insights.claim: The article frames revenue-based ratios as reflecting past investment decisions while capex-based ratios highlight business-model shifts and forward investment, meaning capex is the more forward-looking indicator of the energy transition inside bank portfolios.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Analysts building their own transition-tracking models should weight capex-based exposure metrics more heavily than revenue-based ones when trying to anticipate future financing flows.
insights.quote: While revenue reflects past investment decisions, capex highlights business model shifts and investments – reflecting the ongoing energy transition.
insights.locator: section 3, capex reveals low-carbon financing tilt

insights.claim: For utility-sector deals specifically, the capex-based ESBR reached 3.0:1 in 2025, nearly double the 1.59:1 revenue-based ratio for the same sector, showing utilities are furthest along in shifting capital plans toward low-carbon even where current revenue still skews fossil.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Utilities are the sector where the capex/revenue gap is starkest -- banks with heavy utility-financing exposure (especially in China and Europe) look better positioned on forward transition metrics than their revenue-based ratios suggest.
insights.quote: The capex-based ratio among deals for utilities issuers reached 3.0:1, compared to a 1.59:1 revenue-based ratio in 2025.
insights.locator: section 3, capex reveals low-carbon financing tilt

insights.claim: Chinese utility deals show the most extreme capex/revenue divergence in the report: a capex-based ratio of 12.7:1 versus just 4.24:1 under the revenue approach, indicating Chinese utilities' investment plans are overwhelmingly low-carbon even though current revenue still includes substantial fossil exposure.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: This is the single most striking transition signal in the piece -- Chinese utility capex is running at nearly 13x low-carbon-to-fossil, suggesting China's power-sector transition is further along on a forward-looking basis than any headline revenue-based ratio captures.
insights.quote: Deals for Chinese utilities aggregate to a capex-based ratio of 12.7:1, far above the 4.24:1 under the revenue approach.
insights.locator: section 3, capex reveals low-carbon financing tilt

insights.claim: More major North American banks adopted the ESBR disclosure framework this year even as their actual financing broadly shifted toward fossil fuels: Bank of Nova Scotia and Royal Bank of Canada joined JPMorgan and Citi in disclosing their own versions of the ratio.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Disclosure adoption and actual financing behavior are decoupling in North America -- more transparency doesn't necessarily correlate with better ratios in the near term, which is itself a useful engagement/advocacy data point.
insights.quote: Bank of Nova Scotia and the Royal Bank of Canada joined JPMorgan and Citi in disclosing their own versions of the ratio.
insights.locator: opening section on ESBR adoption

insights.claim: The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) published its ESBR methodology this year but has not yet published an actual ratio, suggesting further North American bank disclosures are likely still to come.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: Watch for CIBC's first published ratio as a near-term disclosure catalyst that could add another North American data point to the ESBR dataset.
insights.quote: The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce also published a methodology this year and has yet to publish a ratio.
insights.locator: opening section on ESBR adoption

insights.claim: The article suggests greater ESBR disclosure may be a precursor to further bank action on their ratios, even though many banks that don't disclose the metric are still posting year-on-year improvements on their own.
insights.speaker: ajacob84
insights.so_what: A speculative but investor-relevant thesis: disclosure pressure (via BNEF's tracking and bank self-reporting) could become a soft lever pushing banks toward higher low-carbon ratios over time, independent of regulation.
insights.quote: Greater disclosure may be the first step toward further action on the ratios, even as many non-disclosing banks continue to post year-on-year improvements.
insights.locator: opening section on ESBR adoption
